title: Word building
intro: Turkmen makes new words by adding endings to old ones, and a handful of endings go a long way. `-lY` means **with** (*şekerli çaý*, tea with sugar) and `-sYz` **without** (*şekersiz*); `-çY` makes a person who works with something (*balykçy*, fisherman); `-lYk` makes abstract nouns (*dostluk*, friendship); `-çA` names languages (*türkmençe*); and `-jYk` makes things small (*kiçijik*, tiny). Learn the endings, and each new noun brings several words with it.

blocks.text: `-lY` turns a noun into a describing word: **with** it, **having** it. It is *-ly* after back vowels and *-li* after front ones: *şeker*, sugar → *şekerli çaý*, tea with sugar; *bulut*, cloud → *bulutly*, cloudy; *akyl*, mind → *akylly*, clever. You already know *bagtly*, happy, from *bagt*, happiness.

**From a place.** On the name of a town or a country, `-lY` says where someone is from, as in [A1 unit 3](a1-u03): *aşgabatly*, from Ashgabat; *maryly*, from Mary; *Siz nireli?* — *Men tejenli.* The spelling rules write these words with a small letter, since they are no longer names; you will also see them with a capital.
*maşynly* means **with a car**, and also **by car**: *Men Aşgabatdan maşynly geldim*, I came from Ashgabat by car.

items.en: Would you like tea with sugar?
It's cloudy today.
Merdan is a very clever boy.
I'm from Ashgabat, but I live in Mary.
Yesterday I came from Ashgabat by car.

blocks.text: `-sYz` is the opposite: **without**. *şekersiz çaý*, tea without sugar; *işsiz*, without work, unemployed; *pulsuz*, free (of charge). Its vowel follows harmony and the rounding rule: *-syz*, *-siz*, and *-suz*, *-süz* after a word of one syllable with *o, ö, u, ü*: *suwsuz*, without water; *gülsüz*, without flowers.
Note the rounding: *duzsuz*, *süýtsüz*, but *duzly*, *süýtli*. A vowel at the very end of a word never rounds, which is why `-lY` stays *-ly*, *-li* after any one-syllable word.

items.en: Tea without sugar for me, please.
The museum is free on Saturday.
The desert is dry and hot.
He is out of work now.

blocks.title: Without, not a negative
blocks.text: `-sYz` makes a describing word, not a negative sentence: *Çaý şekersiz*, the tea is without sugar. For **there is no sugar**, use *ýok*: *Şeker ýok*.

`-çY` makes a noun for the person who works with something, makes it or sells it: *balyk*, fish → *balykçy*, fisherman; *haly* → *halyçy*, carpet weaver; *iş* → *işçi*, worker; *çörek* → *çörekçi*, baker; *aýdym* → *aýdymçy*, singer. You know *okuwçy*, pupil, from *okuw*, studies. The *ç* never changes, and the final *k* of the noun stays: *balykçy*, *çörekçi*.
**From a verb** the ending is `-(Y)jY` instead: *satmak* → *satyjy*, seller; *sürmek* → *sürüji*, driver; *ýazmak* → *ýazyjy*, writer. `-çY` goes on nouns, `-(Y)jY` on verbs: *sürüji*, not `sürçi`.

items.en: My grandfather is a fisherman.
This baker's bread is very good.
The singer sang two songs at the wedding.
The writer is writing a new book.

blocks.title: Jobs with to be
blocks.text: With **to be**, a job takes no word for **a**: *Men işçi*, I'm a worker; *Ejäm halyçy*, my mother is a carpet weaver.

`-lYk` makes nouns. On an adjective or a noun it often makes an abstract noun, like English **-ness**, **-ship** or **-dom**: *dost*, friend → *dostluk*, friendship; *gözel*, beautiful → *gözellik*, beauty; *garaşsyz*, independent → *garaşsyzlyk*, independence; *ýalňyş*, wrong → *ýalňyşlyk*, mistake. You met *çagalyk*, childhood, in [A2 unit 2](a2-u02), and *Garaşsyzlyk baýramy*, Independence Day, in its interlude.
*sag*, healthy, gives *saglyk*, health. It also makes amounts of time: *sagat*, hour → *bir sagatlyk ýol*, a one-hour journey; *iki günlük iş*, two days' work.

**Spelling.** The vowel follows harmony and the rounding rule: *dostluk*, rounded after one syllable with *o* or *ö*; *saglyk*, *gözellik*, *garaşsyzlyk*. The *k* becomes *g* before a vowel: *dostlugy*, *saglygyňyz*, your health.

items.en: To our friendship!
To your health!
Sorry for the mistake.
It's a one-hour journey.

blocks.title: Which one: -lyk or -ly?
blocks.text: *-ly* describes: *akylly adam*, a clever person. *-lyk* names: *dostluk*, friendship. One letter makes a different word, so read the end carefully.

`-çA` on the name of a people gives the language, and **in** that language: *türkmen* → *türkmençe*, Turkmen, in Turkmen; *iňlis* → *iňlisçe*; *rus* → *rusça*; *nemes* → *nemesçe*; *fransuz* → *fransuzça*. You know two of them from [A1 unit 6](a1-u06): *Türkmençe gürleýärsiňizmi?*

*türkmen dili*, the Turkmen language, is the noun, a compound from [A2 unit 10](a2-u10); *türkmençe* says how, in what language: *Men türkmen dilini öwrenýärin*, I'm learning Turkmen; *Türkmençe ýaz*, write in Turkmen.
On a possessive, `-çA` means **according to**: *meniň pikirimçe*, in my opinion (literally, by my thought); *seniň pikiriňçe*, in your opinion. *Maňa görä* ([A2 unit 9](a2-u09)) means the same.

items.en: Do you speak Russian?
This book is in German.
In my opinion, this film is good.
Please speak slowly in Turkmen.

blocks.text: Two endings make things small, or say them with affection. `-jYk`, *-jyk* or *-jik*: *kiçi*, small → *kiçijik*, tiny; *çaga* → *çagajyk*, little child; *oglan* → *oglanjyk*, little boy; *towşan*, hare → *towşanjyk*, little hare. `-jAgAz`, *-jagaz* or *-jegez*, is warmer still and frequent in stories: *gyz* → *gyzjagaz*, little girl; *oglan* → *oglanjagaz*, little lad.

You know *azajyk*, a little, from [A2 unit 8](a2-u08): it is *az*, few, made small. The grammar of the explanatory dictionary groups these endings with *-ja* (*akja*, whitish) as endings of degree: they make a word a little smaller or softer without changing what it is.

They suit children, small animals and things you are fond of, and in tales they set the tone: *Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken, bir gyzjagaz bar eken.* Not every noun takes them; learn the forms as words when you meet them.

items.en: This tiny house is ours.
The little girl is helping her mother.
The little boy is crying.
A little hare came out of the garden.

blocks.title: Tiny or smaller?
blocks.text: *kiçijik* is **tiny**; *kiçiräk* ([A2 unit 8](a2-u08)) is **smaller**, **rather small**. `-jYk` shrinks a word; `-rAk` compares.

summary: `-lY` means **with, having**, or **from** a place: *şekerli çaý*, *bulutly*, *akylly*, *aşgabatly*; *maşynly*, by car.
`-sYz` means **without**: *şekersiz*, *işsiz*, *pulsuz*; *suwsuz*, *süýtsüz* round after *o, ö, u, ü*.
`-çY` makes a person who works with something: *balykçy*, *halyçy*, *işçi*, *çörekçi*; on verbs, `-(Y)jY`: *satyjy*, *ýazyjy*.
`-lYk` makes nouns: *dostluk*, *gözellik*, *garaşsyzlyk*, *ýalňyşlyk*, *saglyk*; amounts of time: *bir sagatlyk ýol*.
`-çA` names languages and says **in** them: *türkmençe*, *rusça*, *nemesçe*; *meniň pikirimçe*, in my opinion.
`-jYk` and `-jAgAz` make things small and dear: *kiçijik*, *oglanjyk*, *gyzjagaz*.
